title: Altered hieroglyphs in Egypt
summary: A scribe uses unusual signs in the tomb of Khnumhotep II.
body: In the tomb of the nobleman Khnumhotep II at Beni Hasan, a scribe substituted uncommon hieroglyphs for familiar ones. David Kahn, in The Codebreakers, treats this as the earliest known deliberate transformation of writing.
The aim was probably dignity and mystery rather than secrecy, but the basic move is already there: replacing one symbol with another.

title: A secret glaze recipe in cuneiform
summary: A Mesopotamian craftsman hides a pottery-glaze recipe on a clay tablet.
body: A clay tablet from Mesopotamia, dated near 1500 BC, records a recipe for pottery glaze, presumably valuable to its owner. The writer replaced the usual cuneiform signs with signs in their least common sound values, and varied the spelling, so that a casual reader could not follow it.
It is a trade secret rather than a state secret: one of the earliest known uses of cryptography to protect commercial knowledge, and an example of hiding text inside a script's own ambiguity.

title: Atbash in the Hebrew Bible
summary: Jeremiah's Sheshach stands for Babel.
body: Atbash mirrors the Hebrew alphabet, swapping first with last. In the Book of Jeremiah, the word Sheshach is widely read as an Atbash form of Babel.
There is no key, so anyone who knows the method can read it. Its importance is that a text-transforming system was already familiar to scribes.

title: The Spartan scytale
summary: A strip wound around a rod scrambles a message.
body: Greek and later Roman writers describe Spartan commanders using a strip of parchment wound around a staff. Plutarch gives the best-known account. Some modern historians doubt how far it was used for secrecy, as opposed to authentication.
Whatever its real use, it is the classic example of transposition, where letters keep their identity but lose their place.

title: Polybius's square
summary: Letters become pairs of numbers, for signalling.
body: The Greek historian Polybius described a grid for sending letters by torch signals. Each letter becomes a row and a column.
Turning a letter into two coordinates is called fractionation, and it returned two thousand years later in ADFGVX and other serious ciphers.

title: Caesar's shift
summary: Suetonius records Julius Caesar shifting letters by three.
body: The Roman biographer Suetonius says Caesar wrote confidential letters by replacing each letter with the one three places further along.
With only a handful of possible shifts it is easy to break by trial, which is exactly what the app's attack does.

title: The Rök runestone
summary: A Swedish runestone encrypts part of its text twice over.
body: The Rök runestone in Östergötland, Sweden, carved about 800 AD, carries the longest known runic inscription. Part of it is encrypted in two ways: by displacement, each rune written as its neighbour in the futhark (a Caesar shift), and by cipher runes that give the number of a rune's ætt and its place in it.

The carver also switches to the older 24-rune futhark, apparently on purpose. Most runologists agree how the runes are deciphered, while the meaning of the text is still debated. Both of its ciphers are in the Library, and they reproduce the stone's resolved passages.

title: Al-Kindi invents frequency analysis
summary: The first written method for breaking substitution ciphers.
body: In Baghdad the polymath Abu Yusuf al-Kindi wrote a manuscript on deciphering cryptographic messages. He observed that letters occur at characteristic rates, so the commonest symbol in a long ciphertext probably stands for the commonest letter of the language.
This is the first recorded general method of cryptanalysis. It made every simple substitution vulnerable, however many keys it had.

title: Secret forms of Ogham
summary: An Irish manuscript lists dozens of variant Ogham alphabets.
body: The Book of Ballymote, written about 1390, contains the Auraicept na n-Éces, a scholars' handbook on the Irish language and on Ogham. Its folios list scores of Ogham variants, numbered and named, alongside the ordinary alphabet.
Some are scholarly games, but the principle matches the Norse cipher runes: keep the familiar strokes and change how they map to letters.

title: Alberti's cipher disk
summary: The first known polyalphabetic cipher.
body: Leon Battista Alberti described two concentric rings of letters. By turning the inner ring during a message, the writer changes alphabets, which flattens the letter frequencies that al-Kindi's method relies on.
This was the most important idea in cryptography for centuries.

title: An author hidden in chapter initials
summary: A Venetian book signs itself with an acrostic.
body: The Hypnerotomachia Poliphili was printed by Aldus Manutius in Venice in December 1499, without an author's name. The first, elaborately decorated letter of each chapter, read in order, spells POLIAM FRATER FRANCISCVS COLVMNA PERAMAVIT: 'Brother Francesco Colonna loved Polia greatly'.

An acrostic of names is hard to find by machine: word lists hold few names, so the app's finder sees it only weakly (16% of its letters in Latin dictionary words, though still more than shuffled letters).

title: Bellaso's keyed tableau
summary: The cipher later misnamed after Vigenere.
body: Giovan Battista Bellaso published a polyalphabetic system driven by a memorable keyword. Blaise de Vigenere described a stronger autokey system in 1586, yet the name Vigenere became attached to Bellaso's method.
It became known as le chiffre indechiffrable, the unbreakable cipher, and kept that reputation for about three centuries.

title: The Babington Plot
summary: A broken cipher sends Mary, Queen of Scots to the block.
body: Letters between Mary and Anthony Babington, plotting against Elizabeth I, used a nomenclator: a substitution alphabet plus code words. Walsingham's cryptanalyst Thomas Phelippes read them.
Mary was executed in 1587. In 2023, researchers decrypted a further 57 of her letters found in the French national library.

title: The Great Cipher of Louis XIV
summary: Unread for two centuries after its makers died.
body: The Rossignol family built a nomenclator for the French court in which numbers stood largely for syllables. Knowledge of it died with them.
Around 1890 the French cryptanalyst Etienne Bazeries broke it, using the guess that a repeated number group meant les ennemis.

title: Jón Ólafsson explains the cipher runes
summary: An Icelandic scholar writes down how Viking cipher runes work.
body: Knowledge of cipher runes survived best in Iceland. In Copenhagen between 1732 and 1752, Jón Ólafsson of Grunnavík wrote the Runologia, a treatise on many cipher runes and runic ciphers, now in the Arnamagnæan Institute.

He gave the Younger Futhark in its Viking-age order, with the m-rune before the l-rune. That detail mattered: every cipher rune names a rune by its group and position, so the wrong order gives the wrong letter.

title: B-A-C-H in The Art of Fugue
summary: Bach writes his own name in notes.
body: In German note names B is B-flat and H is B-natural, so the name Bach can be played: B-flat, A, C, B-natural. Johann Sebastian Bach used the motif in several works, most famously as the third and last subject of the final, unfinished fugue of The Art of Fugue.
It is a signature rather than a secret, and it became the most imitated musical cryptogram: later composers wrote fugues and tributes on the same four notes.

title: Jefferson's wheel
summary: A cylinder of lettered discs, rediscovered a century later.
body: Thomas Jefferson described a stack of independently turning discs. Dial a line of plaintext, then send any other line.
The idea was reinvented by Etienne Bazeries, and the US Army adopted a similar M-94 device in 1922.

title: Champollion reads hieroglyphs
summary: The Rosetta Stone opens ancient Egypt.
body: Jean-Francois Champollion, building on work including Thomas Young's, showed that hieroglyphs combine sound signs and meaning signs.
It remains the model for how lost scripts are read: a bilingual text and a known related language. Most scripts in the Lost Scripts Lab have neither.

title: Schumann's Abegg Variations
summary: A young composer turns a name into a theme.
body: Robert Schumann's Op. 1, written as a student in Heidelberg in 1829 and 1830, is a set of variations on a theme spelled A-B-E-G-G in notes. Schumann used such cryptograms all his life: Carnaval is built on A-S-C-H (A, E-flat, C, B-natural), the name of a town.
The German note names make these spellings exact: each letter that is a note name becomes that note.

title: Wheatstone's Playfair cipher
summary: Pairs of letters, not single letters.
body: Charles Wheatstone invented the digraph cipher later promoted by Lord Playfair. It was used by the British in the Boer War and in the First World War as a field cipher.
Enciphering pairs hides single-letter frequencies, but digraph statistics remain.

title: Kasiski breaks the Vigenere
summary: Repeats reveal the length of the key.
body: Friedrich Kasiski published a general method: repeated sequences in a ciphertext tend to be separated by multiples of the key length. Charles Babbage had found similar ideas earlier but did not publish.
Once the key length is known, each column is a simple Caesar shift. The unbreakable cipher was finished.

title: Kerckhoffs's principle
summary: Assume the enemy knows the system.
body: Auguste Kerckhoffs argued that a military cipher must stay secure even if the system falls into enemy hands. Only the key should be secret.
It is still the foundation of modern cryptography.

title: The Beale Papers are published
summary: Three number ciphers and a promised treasure.
body: A pamphlet claimed that three ciphers revealed the location of buried gold in Virginia. The second opened using the Declaration of Independence as a book key.
The other two remain unread, and many suspect a hoax. This app reproduces the Beale 2 decoding and tests the others.

title: Elgar's Enigma Variations
summary: A theme said to hide a larger, unnamed theme.
body: Edward Elgar composed his Variations on an Original Theme between October 1898 and February 1899; it was first performed in London on 19 June 1899. Each variation portrays one of his friends.

Elgar said the main theme, which he called 'Enigma', referred in some way to a larger, unspecified theme. He never revealed it, and the many proposed solutions have not been confirmed. Elgar is also the author of the Dorabella cipher in the Mystery Lab.

title: Ravel and the French note cipher
summary: Composers spell HAYDN for the centenary.
body: For the centenary of Joseph Haydn in 1909 the journal S.I.M. invited composers to write pieces on his name. The 'French' method writes the alphabet in rows of seven under the notes A to G; for HAYDN the H was kept as B-natural, giving B, A, D, D, G. Maurice Ravel's Menuet sur le nom d'Haydn is the best known result.
Because three or four letters share each note, the French method spells names easily but reads back only by guessing which letters were meant.

title: The Zimmermann Telegram
summary: A decoded telegram helps bring America into the war.
body: Britain's Room 40 decrypted a German proposal offering Mexico an alliance against the United States.
Its publication helped turn American opinion, and the United States entered the war weeks later. It remains the classic case of codebreaking altering history.

title: Painvin breaks ADFGVX
summary: Fractionation meets a brilliant French analyst.
body: Germany introduced ADFGX and then ADFGVX for its spring offensives. Georges Painvin's solutions in June 1918 gave the Allies warning of an attack.
The system combines Polybius-style coordinates with a transposition.

title: Vernam's teleprinter cipher
summary: The road to the one-time pad.
body: Gilbert Vernam of AT&T combined teleprinter characters with a key tape. With Joseph Mauborgne's insistence on random, never-reused keys, this became the one-time pad.
Claude Shannon later proved it unbreakable when used correctly.

title: Rejewski breaks Enigma
summary: Polish mathematicians crack the machine.
body: Marian Rejewski used permutation theory to reconstruct the wiring of German military Enigma. With Henryk Zygalski and Jerzy Rozycki he built methods and machines to read traffic.
In July 1939 Poland shared these results with Britain and France, weeks before the invasion.

title: The bombe at Bletchley Park
summary: Turing and Welchman mechanise the search.
body: Alan Turing designed an electromechanical machine to test Enigma settings against a guessed fragment of plaintext. Gordon Welchman's diagonal board made it far stronger.
A wrong guess leads to a contradiction and can be thrown out at once. Run the same idea in the app.

title: The Purple cipher is broken
summary: American analysts rebuild a machine they had never seen.
body: William Friedman's team, including Frank Rowlett and Genevieve Grotjan, reconstructed Japan's diplomatic cipher machine from its traffic alone.
Their replica machines gave US leaders the intelligence known as Magic.

title: The Navajo code talkers
summary: A language as a code.
body: US Marines recruited Navajo speakers to send messages in a coded form of their language during the Pacific War. It was fast and was never broken.
It shows that a code's strength can come from language itself, a theme that returns with undeciphered scripts.

title: Tutte, Flowers and Colossus
summary: Breaking Lorenz leads to a programmable electronic computer.
body: After an operator's mistake gave Bletchley a depth in 1941, John Tiltman recovered key and Bill Tutte deduced the structure of a machine nobody had seen.
Tommy Flowers then built Colossus, among the first electronic programmable computers, to automate the attack.

title: Project Venona
summary: A reused one-time pad exposes Soviet spies.
body: US and British analysts found that wartime Soviet pads had been duplicated. Decades of work read thousands of messages and exposed agents.
The cipher was perfect in theory. Human reuse was the weakness.

title: The D-Day crossword scare
summary: Invasion codewords turn up as crossword answers.
body: Between 2 May and 1 June 1944 the Daily Telegraph crossword's answers included UTAH, OMAHA, OVERLORD, MULBERRY and NEPTUNE, all secret codewords for the Normandy landings. MI5 questioned the setter, the headmaster Leonard Dawe, and a colleague, and found them innocent. The explanation that emerged: Dawe had pupils fill crossword grids with words, which he then clued, and war-related words, the codenames among them, found their way in.

The lesson for codebreakers: a coincidence too unlikely to be chance (under any word-frequency model these five words in one month are vanishingly rare) is not thereby a secret message. The cause was real, but it was a common source, not espionage.
links: Lens (check a text for hidden messages)

title: Shannon founds modern cryptography
summary: Secrecy becomes mathematics.
body: Claude Shannon's Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems introduced confusion, diffusion and unicity distance, and proved the one-time pad perfectly secret.
Unicity distance is why this app can say that some short mysteries cannot have a unique solution.

title: Shostakovich's D-S-C-H
summary: A composer's monogram in his quartets and symphonies.
body: Dmitri Shostakovich used the German note names for his motto D-Es-C-H: D, E-flat, C, B-natural, standing for D. Sch(ostakowitsch) in German spelling. It appears in his Tenth Symphony, several string quartets and other works, and in every movement of the Eighth String Quartet.
Like Bach's, the motto is a personal signature written into the music for those who know how to read it.

title: Linear B and Maya break open
summary: Ventris reads Mycenaean Greek, and Knorozov opens Maya.
body: Michael Ventris, building on Alice Kober's patient analysis, showed that Linear B writes an early form of Greek. In the same year Yuri Knorozov published the key insight that Maya writing has phonetic signs.
Linear A, closely related to Linear B in script but not in language, is still unread.

title: The VIC cipher revealed
summary: A Soviet spy's cipher falls only to a defector.
body: Reino Hayhanen defected and explained the elaborate pencil-and-paper cipher used by Soviet agents. Analysts had not been able to break it.
It combined a straddling checkerboard, chain addition and double transposition.

title: Schoolteachers crack the Zodiac's Z408
summary: Donald and Bettye Harden read a killer's cipher.
body: A homophonic cipher sent by the Zodiac killer was solved by a California schoolteacher and his wife within days.
It is now a standard test for automated solvers, including this app's.

title: Public-key cryptography
summary: Diffie, Hellman, and then RSA.
body: Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman showed that two parties could agree a secret over an open channel. Rivest, Shamir and Adleman followed with RSA.
British intelligence had found equivalent ideas earlier: Clifford Cocks described RSA-like encryption at GCHQ in 1973, kept secret until the 1990s.

title: DES and Deep Crack
summary: A public standard, and its fall to brute force.
body: The Data Encryption Standard made strong cryptography a public matter. Its 56-bit key was criticised from the start.
In 1998 the Electronic Frontier Foundation's Deep Crack machine found a DES key in days.

title: AES is chosen
summary: An open competition produces today's standard.
body: NIST selected Rijndael, by Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen, through a public international contest.
No practical attack on the full cipher is known. Real failures come from misuse, shown in the app's attack pages.

title: The Copiale cipher falls
summary: Computers read an 18th-century secret-society manuscript.
body: Kevin Knight, Beata Megyesi and Christiane Schaefer showed that the 105-page Copiale cipher hid German text from an Enlightenment secret society, with statistical methods at the heart of the work.
It showed what careful computational cryptanalysis can do for historical documents.

title: Z340 is solved after 51 years
summary: A transposition hidden in a homophonic cipher.
body: David Oranchak, Sam Blake and Jarl Van Eycke solved the Zodiac's 340-character cipher, using heavy computation and the discovery of a diagonal transposition.
This app reproduces the period-19 signal, but has not read the letters.

title: Mary, Queen of Scots's lost letters
summary: Fifty-seven letters read after four centuries.
body: George Lasry, Norbert Biermann and Satoshi Tomokiyo found ciphered letters misfiled in the French national library, and decrypted them using computational methods.
The letters come from her years of captivity in England.

title: Post-quantum standards
summary: Preparing for computers that do not exist yet.
body: A large quantum computer running Shor's algorithm would break RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography. NIST published its first post-quantum standards in 2024.

title: Kryptos K4 sold
summary: The solution to the CIA sculpture's last passage goes to auction.
body: Jim Sanborn's Kryptos archive, including the K4 solution, sold at RR Auction in November 2025. The plaintext has not been published.
This app decodes K1 to K3 and rules out a large family of models for K4.
